rationale: A wins because it carves the same fact pattern into three genuinely different reported stories: P&L, driver bill, and connector/interoperability. Its strongest line is "Rivian adds Tesla-style plugs and opens its network with no automaker partner in sight" because that is a beat reporter's actual question, not a slogan. B has a good finance angle, but "Rivian charges rival-brand drivers more..." and "Rivian keeps owners cheaper..." are mostly the same pricing fact wearing two jackets.
gaps_in_A: "no automaker partner in sight" is a shade stronger than the supplied fact "no partnership with another automaker announced"; keep the absence framed as a question unless Rivian confirms it chose to go alone.
"whether 'improves utilization' is a polite way of saying stalls sit empty" is a useful reporter question, but it needs to stay a question; the update gives no underuse baseline.
The consumer angle asks for completed-session proof, but it could also demand basic geography/site coverage; "3,500+ chargers" is less useful without where they are.
gaps_in_B: "Rivian charges rival-brand drivers more..." and "Rivian keeps owners cheaper..." split the same two-tier-pricing fact into two angles; that is padding, not structure.
"Tesla Supercharger access, Electrify America, the NACS transition" imports comparison context not supplied in the update; usable only after sourcing, not as if it came with the facts.
"the way it has for one walled competitor" is coy unsourced Tesla shorthand. Name and source it or kill it.
"cost to retrofit stalls with dual connectors" assumes retrofit economics when the supplied fact only says all new stalls will include CCS and NACS.
